About: Simultaneity on a Minkowski Diagram

Source

Lecture
8 — Lightcone
Simulation
Simulation 1 — Relativity of simultaneity on a Minkowski diagram (guided-inquiry)
Concept
Two events simultaneous in one inertial frame (same ct) are generally not simultaneous in a different inertial frame — shown by the tilt of the primed (S′) coordinate axes.
Serves
Lightcone structure (axes tilt toward the 45° light line); the relativity of simultaneity (core); reading causal structure off a spacetime diagram; spacelike separation as what permits frame-dependent time-ordering.
Inquiry
How does Δct′ depend on Δx and v/c? Can Δct′ change sign (B before A)? When does Δct′ vanish?
Misconception
"They only look non-simultaneous in S′ because light from A and B takes different times to reach the observer — correct for travel time and they're simultaneous again."

Welcome toSimultaneity on a Minkowski diagram

Two events at the same time in one frame. Boost to a frame moving past, and read the times it gives them.

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two events, two frames

Let’s set the scene. Here’s a Minkowski diagram of frame S: position x runs horizontally, time ct vertically, and the dashed 45° lines are light rays through the origin. Events A and B are both at ct = 3 but at different x, so in S they happen at the same time — Δct = 0. A second frame S′ moves along x at speed v = βc and gives each event a time coordinate ct′ of its own.

2 · Simultaneous in every frame?

Here’s the big question. A and B happen at the same instant in S. In frame S′, moving along x, do you think they still happen at the same instant?

Now try raising v/c away from zero: watch the S′ axes tilt and the two ct′ labels split apart.

3 · What sets the size of the disagreement

Now let’s see what sets the size of that disagreement. S′ now moves at v/c = 0.60, and A and B have different ct′. Suppose B is dragged toward A until their separation Δx is one tenth of its present value, still at ct = 3. What do you think happens to Δct′?

Go ahead and drag B toward A, and watch Δct′ shrink with Δx; bring them to the same x and it reaches zero.

4 · Which event comes first

Now let’s look at the order. At v/c = +0.60 the diagram gives ct′B < ct′A: in S′, B — the event further along the boost direction — happens first. What do you predict the same pair does at v/c = −0.60?

Now set v/c to −0.60 and read ct′A and ct′B again to check.

5 · Does cause and effect survive

That raises a worrying question. A and B are spacelike separated: each lies outside the other’s light cone, the dashed 45° lines, and their order in S′ depends on the boost. So what do you think — can a boost also reverse the order of a cause and its effect?

Press ▶ Play to sweep v/c and watch: Δct′ swings through zero and changes sign, while Δs² never moves.

6 · The relativity of simultaneity

So here’s what you’ve discovered. Two events sharing a time in one frame share a time in another only if they happen at the same place. That’s the relativity of simultaneity — not a measurement error, and no threat to cause and effect, since only spacelike pairs can swap order.

β = v/c · γ = 1/√(1 − β²)
ct′ = γ(ct − βx) · Δct′ = −γβΔx whenever Δct = 0
Δs² = −Δct² + Δx² — frame-invariant; Δs² > 0 is spacelike

The Physics

Simultaneity on a Minkowski diagram · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim draws two events on the spacetime diagram of frame S and shows the times a second frame S′, moving along x, assigns to them. It is about what the two frames agree on and what they do not.

What you'll learn

  • How to read a time in S′ off the tilted S′ axes of the diagram.
  • How the times S′ assigns to the two events depend on the boost v/c and on their separation Δx.
  • How the order of the two events in S′ depends on the direction of the boost.
  • What the interval Δs² is, and how it sorts pairs of events.
Frame S (pale axes) and frame S′ (teal axes). A and B are level: the same ct in S. Not to scale.

What's on screen

  • Event A (blue) and event B (rose), each labelled with (x, ct). Drag either one sideways.
  • Pale axes and grid: frame S, with x across and ct up in the same unit.
  • Teal axes ct′ and x′: frame S′, with squares at whole units and a faint dashed grid.
  • Dashed yellow lines: light rays at 45° through the origin.
  • Dashed lines from A and B to the ct′ axis. The label there is that event's ct′.
  • Corner box: v/c and Δct′. Readings panel: the full numbers for both frames.
See itShow the diagram with S′ at its opening v/c = 0.60. Watch for: A and B level with each other, and the teal S′ axes leaning toward the yellow light line.

03

The S′ axes lean toward the light lines

S′ moves along x at speed v = βc. Its time axis ct′ is the path of its own origin, the line x = β ct, and its space axis x′ is the line ct = βx.

β is the speed of S′ measured in S, as a fraction of c.
  • Light must travel at c in S′ as well. A light ray at 45° stays at 45°, so the ct′ and x′ axes lean toward the same light line, one from each side.
  • This is not a Euclidean rotation. A rotation would turn both axes the same way and keep them at 90° on the page. Here the axes close together like scissor blades.
  • Each axis tilts by arctan β from its S counterpart: 31° at β = 0.60, 42° at β = 0.90. For |β| < 1 it never reaches the light line.
See itSet v/c to 0.90. Watch for: the teal ct′ and x′ axes leaning close to the same light line from opposite sides, without touching it.
04

A time in S′ is read along a line of constant ct′

An event at (x, ct) in S has coordinates (x′, ct′) in S′. With c = 1, the sim computes:

The boost from S to S′. It is derived in Lecture 10; here, read what it does to the axes.
  • ct′ is a clock reading, not an arrival time. It is what a clock at rest in S′, sitting at the event and synchronised with the other clocks of S′, reads there. Light-travel delays are already removed.
  • Events with the same ct′ lie on a line parallel to the x′ axis. The sim draws that line from each event to the ct′ axis and prints the value there.
The two axes, and the line of constant ct′ through any event.

The label sits at height γ·ct′ on S's scale, because the tick marks on the S′ axes are spaced wider than those on S. Read the number, not the height.

See itFollow each dashed line from its event to the ct′ axis. Watch for: the blue and rose lines running parallel to the teal x′ axis, and the ct′ values printed where they meet the ct′ axis.
05

Equal times in S become unequal in S′

A and B share one ct in S, so Δct = 0. Put that into the boost and one term drops out:

Δct′ = ct′B − ct′A and Δx = xB − xA, in units where c = 1.
v/c Δx

The v/c slider here is the sim's slider. Δx changes when you drag A or B.

  • Δct′ is proportional to Δx. It needs both a boost (β ≠ 0) and a separation (Δx ≠ 0); lacking either, it is zero.
  • It grows with β through γβ, which is 0.31, 0.75 and 2.06 at β = 0.30, 0.60 and 0.90. Doubling β more than doubles it.
The same two events at β = 0 and at the opening β = 0.60. A is at x = −1.50 and B at x = 2.53, both at ct = 3.
See itAt v/c = 0.60, bring B toward A: to half, then a tenth of its Δx. Watch for: Δct′ falling in step with Δx, to half and then a tenth of its first value.
06

Reversing the boost reverses the order

Δct′ = −γβΔx changes sign when β does, with the same size. The event further along the boost direction is the earlier one in S′.

Same events, opposite boosts. The dashed lines are lines of constant ct′ through each event.
  • At β = +0.60, S′ moves toward +x and B is further along: ct′B = 1.85 comes before ct′A = 4.88, so B is first. At β = −0.60, A is first.
  • In S′ the clocks of S move toward −x, so the clock at A leads. A moving array's leading clock reads behind its trailing ones, so A's reading of 3 happens later in S′.
  • Only β = 0 or Δx = 0 gives a tie.
See itRun v/c = +0.60, then v/c = −0.60, on the same two events. Watch for: Δct′ changing sign, and the card naming the first event each time.
07

Only some pairs can swap order

This sim uses Δs² = −Δct² + Δx² (with c = 1), so a spacelike pair has Δs² > 0: no signal, even one at c, can join its two events. Δs² has the same value in S and in S′.

The interval is the same number in both frames. The sim prints both in Readings.
  • For a spacelike pair, a boost can change the order (section 06). For a timelike pair (Δs² < 0) or a null pair (Δs² = 0) it cannot: then |Δx| ≤ |Δct|, so βΔx can never outweigh Δct, and Δct′ = γ(Δct − βΔx) keeps the sign of Δct.
  • In this sim A and B always share ct, so Δs² = +Δx² and the pair is spacelike for any Δx ≠ 0. The sim shows the order swapping, but cannot show a pair that keeps its order.
The lines of constant ct′ through A for every boost the sim allows (|β| ≤ 0.9). They stay inside the spacelike region.

The yellow lines the sim draws are the light cone of the origin, not of A or B. "Spacelike" here describes the pair A and B.

See itPress Play to sweep v/c while Readings is open. Watch for: Δct′ swinging through zero and changing sign, while both Δs² values hold still.
08

Where it matters

  • Why signals cannot exceed c. A signal faster than light would join a spacelike pair, and in some frame it would arrive before it was sent. This is the standard argument for c as the limit on signals.
  • Synchronising clocks in a moving frame. Clocks synchronised in S, as read from S′, are offset by vΔx/c² at low speed. For a jet at 250 m/s and two points 100 m apart that is 0.28 ps: real, and far too small to see.
  • GPS. Receivers work in an Earth-fixed frame that rotates, and GPS timing includes the Sagnac correction, an offset of the same form: velocity times distance over c². The rotating Earth is not an inertial frame, so the sim's two frames are only an analogy here.
Go deeper: the offset in ordinary units
  • Putting c back, two events simultaneous in S and Δx apart are Δt′ = −γvΔx/c² apart in S′.
  • γ is close to 1 until v is a sizeable fraction of c (it is 1.25 at 0.6c), so at everyday speeds the offset is just vΔx/c².
09

Summary

In one line. Two events at the same time in S but at different places get different times in S′, by Δct′ = −γβΔx. For a spacelike pair the order depends on the frame, and Δs² does not.

Key points

  • Δct′ = −γβΔx is zero only if β = 0 or Δx = 0.
  • The event further along the boost direction is first in S′. Reversing the boost reverses the order.
  • Δs² = −Δct² + Δx² is the same in S and S′. Only spacelike pairs (Δs² > 0) can swap order.

Common mix-ups

  • "They only look non-simultaneous because light from A and B reaches S′ at different times." A time coordinate is a synchronised clock reading, so the gap survives every delay correction.
  • "There is one real 'now', and the frames just measure it badly." Each frame's lines of constant ct′ slice spacetime equally validly.
  • "If the order can flip, cause and effect are in danger." Only spacelike pairs can flip. Pairs a signal can join keep their order in every frame.

Things to try on your own

  • Drag B onto A so that Δx = 0, then sweep v/c with Play and read Δct′.
  • Compare Δct′ at v/c = 0.30 and 0.60 for the same Δx, and explain the ratio with γβ.
  • Open Readings, drag A or B, and check that Δs² in S and in S′ still agree.
